title: Post-kindle checks on a doe and her litter
subtitle: What to check in the nest box and on the doe in the first 48 hours after kindling.
excerpt: The first 48 hours after a doe kindles are the highest-risk period for both the doe and the kits. Still-born kits, a doe that has not cleared all the afterbirth, kits that are not being fed, or a litter scattered outside the nest can all be addressed quickly if caught early. A few minutes of careful observation twice a day in the first week saves most problems that would otherwise become losses.
sourceNotes: British Rabbit Council, Doe and Litter Management Guidelines (2022). RSPCA, Rabbit breeding and litter care (2023). Patrice Moreau-Sipiere, Rabbit husbandry and health: a guide for practitioners (2017). RWAF, Rabbit litter welfare notes (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: The act of giving birth in rabbits. Most does kindle during the night or early morning; birth is rapid (often completed in under 30 minutes) and the doe may eat the placenta.
A newborn rabbit. Kits are born hairless, blind, and deaf, and are entirely dependent on the doe for warmth and feeding during the first two to three weeks of life.

Assessment of whether a doe is producing milk. Gently press the skin of the abdomen near a teat: if a small drop of milk can be expressed, she is producing. Doe rabbits feed their kits once or twice per day in one brief session, often at night.

content.text: needs two checks on her first day and twice daily for the rest of the first week. The checks are quick and minimally disturbing if done calmly, and they are the most reliable way to avoid losing kits to preventable causes in the highest-risk period.
First check: immediately after discovery of kindling
Count the kits in the nest box. Note any kits outside the nest box: kits are born inside or near the nest, but can be scattered if the doe kindled while moving around the cage.
Remove any stillborn kits. A stillborn kit is cold, flat, and does not respond to touch. Remove them promptly to avoid the doe distressing herself and the remaining kits.
Check for retained kits: if the doe seems distressed or is straining with no kit appearing after 30 to 60 minutes, this is a retained kit and a vet call.

Warm any chilled kit: a kit that feels cold to the touch but moves slightly when held can often be revived by holding it against your body for 10 to 15 minutes to warm it. Once warm, return it to the nest.
Check the doe. Look at the vulva for signs of heavy bleeding (a small amount of discharge is normal). Check all teats are accessible and not damaged. Gently check
Daily checks for the first week
are warm, rounded (full bellies have a distinct dome shape; hungry kits are wrinkled and flat-sided), and grouped in the nest rather than scattered.
Check the doe's appetite and water intake. A doe nursing a large litter has high water needs; a dehydrated doe produces less milk.
Check the nest box for soiled or wet bedding. Wet bedding in winter chills the kits rapidly. Replace damp hay with dry hay as needed.

From day 10, check that eyes are beginning to open (expected from day 10 to 12). Eyes that remain sealed past day 14 and appear sticky or crusty need gentle cleaning and possibly vet review for infection.

Does feed their kits in very brief sessions, typically once or twice in 24 hours and often at night. If you observe the nest and never see the doe feeding, this does not mean she is not feeding. The sign that kits are being fed is their round, full bellies, check this rather than watching for feeding behaviour.

attrs.cue: Kits consistently thin and wrinkled by the morning check despite the doe appearing healthy
attrs.cause: Doe not producing enough milk, or kits not accessing the teats
attrs.fix: Confirm milk supply by gently expressing a teat. If milk is present, confine the doe in the nest box for a supervised feed session (10 minutes) twice daily. If no milk can be expressed by day 2, the doe may need supplemental kits moved to a wet nurse with a smaller litter.

attrs.cue: Kit found cold and flat outside the nest
attrs.cause: Carried out of the nest attached to a teat, or born late and missed the nest
attrs.fix: Warm the kit against the body. If it regains movement within 20 minutes, return to the nest. A kit that remains cold and unresponsive after 30 minutes of warming is unlikely to recover.
